In brief

This series puts forward an idea that the series has illustrated but leaves untested: the kind of thing a mind wants shapes the kind of conflict it gets into. Here I set out a plan for testing that idea, not a finding. It would test it on historical state leaders and on small AI agents trained in simulated games, and so far no data have been collected and nothing has been run. Each of the plan’s six hypotheses can lose, under rules fixed before anyone reads the data used to judge the hypotheses. On the archive counts expected, the main historical test can lose but cannot be supported. Because the archive’s yield of heirs and the machine coders’ checks are questions to measure rather than assume, the plan’s practical conclusion is to fund a feasibility stage first.

Part 1. The idea under test, and why it needs a test it could fail

Why what a machine wants could matter

Wars happen even though fighting is costly. The bargaining theory of war starts from two premises: the sides want conflicting things over some disputed issue, and war is costly and risky. It then shows how rational sides can still end up fighting. They do so through private information, through problems of commitment, and over stakes that cannot be divided (Fearon 1995; Powell 2006).

In The War Baseline, my paper applying that theory to the arrival of a capable machine, I find one route to war hard to escape. This is the commitment problem across a large shift in power. A side about to gain a large advantage cannot credibly promise not to use it. That gives the side about to fall behind a reason to strike first, while it still can.

In Ends, Rank and Conflict, my paper on what minds want and the conflicts they enter, I argue that what a mind wants is the one premise people might choose in a machine. A person’s aims come from biological evolution, while a machine’s come from its training design. In the technical papers these aims are called “ends”, and I say “aims” here.

That opens a conditional possibility. If the type of aim changes the type of conflict and the training objective determines the aims a machine learns to pursue, then choosing that objective is a real lever on the shape of the risk. The practical question then becomes which aims to install and which to avoid.

The examples that suggested the idea cannot test it

In Ends, Rank and Conflict, I propose a conjecture, an idea to be tested. The conjecture is that the type of a mind’s aims shapes the type of conflict it enters. I leave it untested there. The case for it there and in Changing the Ends rests on historical illustration and theoretical judgment. In the latter, I examine instrumental convergence, the idea that almost any open-ended aim pushes an agent to gather resources and seek power, and close with a sketch of this test.

The cases that suggested an idea cannot also test it. So every person named as an illustration when the conjecture was formed is left out of the test itself. They are held apart as a set for developing the methods.

This is a research design. No data have been collected, no experiment has been run, and no hypothesis is established. It asks one question. Can the conjecture be tested without rediscovering its own illustrations, or building its conclusion into its measures?

Each hypothesis in the design can lose, but a loss would not show that aims do not matter. As an analogy, not one in the technical paper: it is like writing down the terms of a bet before the cards are dealt.

Five problems the design has to solve

  1. A rival for every claim. Each claim must be paired with a prediction from the rival account it has to beat. Rules fixed in advance must be able to register a loss.
  2. Fair sampling, separate measurement. Leaders must be sampled without choosing them for fame. Their aims must be read from records made before the outcome window opens. For the main test of heirs that means before office. A separate team measures what leaders actively sought and gained and how they used violence, against what their office normally saw.
  3. A comparison that could show cause. Aims are never assigned at random, and ambitious people seek power. The design needs a comparison that could identify a causal difference. It also has to say plainly what other people’s strategic responses can do to that comparison.
  4. Machines that cannot be blinded. For one hypothesis the main coders are language models. A model that has read the biographies cannot be kept from knowing how a reign ended. So the design replaces the assumption of blindness with a sequence of checks.
  5. What the attainable study can conclude. The archive and the budget limit what can be learned. That leads to a fallback rule, fixed in advance, for when the archive holds too few cases, and to a feasibility stage before the main money is spent.

What the conjecture says

Ends, Rank and Conflict does not sort minds into boxes. It describes aims along eight dimensions, and this design uses six of them. Five are coded for historical people, and one is varied in the machine experiments. Several ideas recur, so each gets a short name here:

  • Rank-seeking aims (the technical term is “positional”) measure success by standing relative to others.
  • Bounded aims have a stopping point, after which more adds nothing.
  • Group-targeting aims (technical term “totalizing”) are satisfied only if a named group is gone, or conforms in identity or belief.
  • Resource aims (technical term “terminal resource ends”) seek land or wealth for their own sake, not as a means.
  • Rival goods are goods where one side’s use takes from another’s, and non-rival goods are goods where it does not.
  • Power conversion (technical term “convertibility”) is how far what a mind gains turns into power to coerce.

The six dimensions used here are rank-seeking, boundedness, group-targeting, rivalry of use, power conversion, and how much a mind needs resources as means, which is coded on the human side. (Resource aims, above, name what an aim is about rather than a dimension.) A seventh named dimension, whether others can be kept from a good, is not coded. I use those dimensions in Ends, Rank and Conflict to draw four broad links:

  • Aims over relative rank go with conquest and coercive killing.
  • Aims that require a named group’s absence go with genocide.
  • Resource aims over land or wealth that others hold go with dispossession, even when the aim never names the victims.
  • Bounded aims over goods that are not rival leave the most room for a bargain, though they do not guarantee one.

Why the historical cases were only illustrations

Ends, Rank and Conflict is explicit that its biographical cases illustrate rather than test, and it gives four reasons:

  • A roster chosen by lasting reputation tilts toward people known for constructive achievement.
  • Everyone on it counted humanity as their own kind.
  • Before the twentieth century no one had the technical means to pursue an aim that could end the species.
  • A survey of historical figures looks for malice, while the danger stressed in AI research is indifference.

Napoleon is the hardest and most instructive case there. He shows that first-rate ability can go with rank-seeking aims. The Jaffa massacre and the campaign in Saint-Domingue show coercive killing without a group-targeting aim.

I also stress there that atrocity has two layers. Planners at the top choose a campaign, and followers below carry it out. Any study of state leaders or eminent minds reaches only the first layer.

The series papers this design rests on are unpublished drafts. They include Measures That Depend on Ends, my paper on how training objectives install and bound what a machine learns to want. Changing the Ends summarizes this design in one page. Here I set out the complete design, for a funder or a methods workshop to judge.

Two claims, each with its own rivals

The conjecture makes two separate claims. The design keeps them apart because they face different rivals.

The first is satiation: does an actor with a bounded aim stop acquiring once it reaches its bound, even when more could be taken? Realist security and commitment accounts doubt it. They hold that actors gather power to protect themselves and lock in bargains, whatever their ultimate goals. Instrumental-convergence accounts doubt it too. They hold that almost any open-ended goal leads to gathering resources and seeking power (Omohundro 2008; Bostrom 2012).

There is also a formal result. In a standard mathematical model of decision-making with finitely many states, Turner and colleagues prove that under certain symmetries in the setting, the best possible strategies tend to seek power for most goals. They conjecture that agents accumulate resources when future rewards count nearly as much as present ones (Turner et al. 2021).

The second claim is typology: does the content of an actor’s aims predict what kind of lethal violence, if any, it uses? The strategic account of mass killing doubts it (Valentino 2004). In that account, kinds of mass killing are sorted by the killers’ immediate policy goals. Leaders choose the form of killing that serves those goals in the situation they face.

Where those policy goals merely restate aims held before the violence, the two accounts predict the same thing. They come apart in one case: where earlier aims predict the type of violence beyond the strategic situation the leader inherited or that arose before their first coded act of violence without their having started it, and beyond five structural factors adapted from Harff (2003).

The design takes three more things from earlier papers. From The War Baseline it takes the severity of the commitment problem. From Changing the Ends it takes a reading of instrumental convergence. The worrying case is a mind that never has enough and does not care about rank, pursuing something like knowledge, where the pursuit uses up rival inputs that pile up over time. So the test asks whether caring nothing for rank protects against conflict in exactly the settings where inputs are rival or where knowledge turns into power.

Last, it takes from Limits, and an Answer, the series’ closing paper, the limit stated there. No source drawn on in the series shows that a machine can be trained to pursue an aim for which there is a point of having enough. Figure 1 links ideas from three earlier papers to the parts of the test they motivate, and sets a fourth paper’s training limit beside the stopping check that leaves it open.

Part 2. Six hypotheses, each set against the account it must beat

Every hypothesis is paired in advance with the scorable prediction of the standard account it has to beat. Sometimes both accounts predict the same thing, or the result is fixed by how the rewards are built. In those cases the design calls the comparison a control or a secondary check, not a test.

H1 and the machine-error checks use an odds ratio. In each group, the odds compare how often the outcome occurs with how often it does not. The odds ratio compares those two groups’ odds. A ratio of 1 means equal odds, and a ratio above 1 means the outcome is more likely in the first group.

H1: Do heirs whose early writings show rank-seeking reach for more?

H1 concerns heads of state or government who reached high office at a time not chosen for their aims. That means hereditary succession, or a succession fixed by rule before a predecessor died a natural death in office. As in the technical paper, I call these people heirs.

H1 compares heirs on two dimensions of what their writings before office state. Heirs whose writings state a bounded aim are predicted to seek holdings beyond what their office normally gained less often than heirs whose writings state an unbounded one. They are also predicted to turn down an offered increase more often. The same prediction holds for heirs whose writings state an aim that is not about rank, set against heirs whose writings state a rank-seeking aim.

Because H1 crosses two dimensions, it gives two comparisons. Only one of them separates the conjecture from every rival.

  • Bounded against unbounded, with rank-seeking held fixed. Instrumental convergence predicts this difference too, since its claim is that unbounded goals drive acquisition (Omohundro 2008). So this comparison tests only whether boundedness read from documents predicts behaviour at all. It is reported as secondary and does not decide H1.
  • Rank-seeking against not, with boundedness held fixed. Here convergence predicts no difference, because two bounded aims are equally bounded. This comparison separates the conjecture from convergence, and Rule 1 scores it. How the two dimensions combine is a secondary comparison.

The rival on the human side is the realist security and commitment argument (Jervis 1978; Fearon 1995; Powell 2006). Taking office changes what outside rivals fear and what the ruler must defend. On this view, a ruler’s gains after taking office track outside threat and opportunity, whatever the ruler says they want. This holds at least where commitments, strategy or technology make expansion the only route to security.

That rival makes a scorable prediction. Compare heirs facing the same outside threat when they take office and in the same position in the political structure before office. A person’s position during their formative years can shape both what they say they want and whether they expand. The rival predicts equal odds for rank-seeking and other heirs, both for seeking gains above the office baseline and for turning down an offer.

Threats that arise during a reign complicate this. If those threats are unrelated to the ruler’s aims, holding accession threat fixed is enough. But a rank-seeking ruler may provoke the very threats that then prompt further expansion. Holding those provoked threats fixed would soak up part of the effect of aims, so Rule 1 scores the total effect at accession threat. A secondary model that adds threats arising during the reign is reported and not scored. When a ruler helped provoke those threats, the security account predicts equal odds only if the comparison also holds those threats fixed. The secondary model also allows a rise in threat to have a different relationship with the outcome for different types of aims.

H2: Among leaders who killed, do earlier aims predict the kind of killing?

H2 tests prediction. It is not a model of when violence starts. It covers state leaders, 1955–2015 first and 1900–1954 second, who used lethal violence beyond their office’s normal record while in power.

Looking only at leaders who killed can bias the result if aims also affect whether violence starts. The design states this as a limit. A broader model that also includes leaders who stayed at their office’s normal level is reported beside the main one, but the main one governs.

H2 codes the main type of violence from behaviour alone, without reading the killer’s motives. It claims that the main aim stated before the violence began predicts that type:

  • rank-seeking aims predict coercive violence;
  • group-targeting aims predict violence that removes people because of their identity;
  • resource aims predict violence that removes people from territory.

In the technical paper, the last two kinds are called “dispossessive”.

Two rival accounts contest H2. The first is the strategic account (Valentino 2004), from which the coercive and dispossessive categories are adapted. A leader’s ongoing occupation or seizure campaign is plausibly the leader’s own doing. So, to keep the strategic situation from soaking up the effect of aims, it is coded as the leader inherited it at accession, or as a situation that began before the leader’s first coded violent act and that the leader did not start. The situation as it stood once violence was under way goes into a secondary model.

The second is the structural account (Harff 2003). It predicts the onset of genocide and politicide—mass killing of groups defined by their politics—in countries already in state failure, from six national factors:

  • earlier genocide or politicide;
  • political upheaval;
  • the ethnic character of the ruling elite;
  • autocracy;
  • openness to trade;
  • an exclusionary elite ideology.

An exclusionary ideology is close to the thing being tested under another name. So the main model uses the first five factors plus the strategic situation, and the sixth enters only a separate “ceiling” model.

The rivals’ prediction is that, once the situation and the five factors are known, earlier aims add nothing. Against Valentino (2004) the deciding prediction is sharper: earlier aims sort the type of violence before any conflict policy exists. The clearest case would be rank-seeking aims predicting coercive rather than dispossessive violence.

Group-targeting aims are rare in every historical sample, at about 4 to 9 cases in the 600-leader sample. That part of the test is too small, and cannot by itself make H2 lose. As a separate check on the measures, eminent creators are expected to show more rank-seeking over credit than over power, as in priority disputes (Merton 1957).

H3: Is a knowledge-seeking machine as aggressive as a resource-seeking one, when knowledge costs scarce inputs?

H3 moves to reinforcement learning: AI agents that learn by trial and error from rewards, several sharing one simulated world. Each agent’s skill when playing alone is held fixed. H3 compares two training objectives:

  • Knowledge with rival inputs, where an agent is rewarded for discovering hidden sites, but each discovery spends an input that runs out. This is the worrying case identified in Changing the Ends.
  • Rival input, where an agent is rewarded for consuming a resource that runs out.

H3 claims that the two match within a margin set in advance, in two ways. They show the same average level of aggression, and aggression rises as fast in both as scarcity rises. Making progress convertible into coercive power also raises aggression as much under one objective as under the other.

The evidence comes from the multi-agent games, not from solo play. Equalizing solo rewards, weapons earning rates and the solo value of each unit when an agent plays alone makes the two objectives match in solo play almost by construction. Solo play therefore only checks the environment.

Three machine-side rival readings sort out which comparisons are tests and which are controls.

  • Scarcity. Leibo and colleagues found that aggression tracks scarcity and the cost of conflict, under a single fixed apple-collecting reward (Leibo et al. 2017). Here that idea is extended to every objective. On the knowledge comparisons it agrees with the conjecture, so H3 is an equivalence check against a naive “knowledge is safe” reading that no cited work holds. In the rank-seeking game, aggression even when resources are plentiful follows directly from how the rank reward is built. That makes the rank game a positive control (a comparison built to show aggression), not a test.
  • “Knowledge is safe.” This is the reading I reject in Changing the Ends. It predicts less aggression, and a smaller effect of power conversion, under the knowledge objective. H3 loses if the whole 95 percent interval for a gap lies outside the margin in either direction. A gap on the opposite side would point to a route to conflict the design has not named.
  • Formal power-seeking. The theorem of Turner et al. (2021) concerns the best possible strategies, not agents that have actually been trained. So H3 does not test power-seeking itself. If trained agents aggressively sought power everywhere to keep their options open, aggression would appear even under pure knowledge, with no rival inputs and no power conversion. That game is a descriptive negative control: a comparison reported to describe behaviour, not to decide H3.

H3b: Does training find the policy of stopping?

H3b runs with no power conversion and no raiding. In these environments doing nothing is free, and every other action carries a small cost. With those costs and no more reward after the bound, stopping at the bound is strictly better than taking any finite positive number of further costly actions. This is Result 10, one of the design’s formal checks (Part 4 explains them).

H3b predicts that once a bounded agent reaches its bound, its further acquisition stays below the stand-in’s level plus a preset margin. The stand-in is trained with no reward under the same cost and takes over from the bounded agent’s exact state at the bound. It is judged separately for each of the four objectives.

H3c: Does stockpiling for security start at the same point for both objectives?

Sometimes rivals can raid what an agent has stored, or progress buys coercive power. Then an agent with enough and an agent that never has enough may stockpile and strike alike, for security rather than for the final goal. Each agent is paid only up to its bound. The same capped reward rule applies at every power-conversion level, with raiding on or off. For the rival-input objective, reward is paid on consumption. So H3c looks at stockpiling before the bound is reached (the technical term is “pre-bound buffering”). This means extra stored inputs, plus any weapons stock taken in raids, beyond what the objective and the rate of use need. Weapons stock earned by progress is left out, because it accrues mechanically.

The machine design runs power conversion at five dose levels, and finds the security threshold: the level at which stockpiling first rises beyond the margin above a starting reference. The design estimates that level from a fitted curve and uses the same margin as H3b. With raiding on, that reference is the same objective’s own stockpiling at zero power conversion. A comparison with the no-reward stand-in is reported beside it and decides nothing. Figure 2 shows how the threshold is read for each objective, and what happens at the scale’s edges.

H3c claims the threshold matches within one dose level between the two objectives. Like H3, it is an equivalence check and does not test formal power-seeking itself. The “knowledge is safe” rival predicts a higher threshold for knowledge. The security account predicts that raiding lowers the threshold measured against the no-reward stand-in, and raises stockpiling and aggression for every objective with a store that can be seized. The conjecture does not dispute this, and it is reported descriptively.

Sometimes there is no threshold inside the scale. An agent may never rise beyond the margin, or may already be beyond it at zero conversion. Such a result can make H3c lose but cannot support it. A preliminary run, called the pilot, estimates how often the threshold runs off the top of the scale.

H3d: A check on the commitment mechanism, not a test of aims

H3d uses a two-agent bargaining game with a scheduled, announced shift in power. It is scored on planning agents that look far enough ahead to see past the shift. Agreements cannot be enforced, and fixed pairings let the declining side learn during training what type of agent the rising side is.

The score compares how much more often the declining side attacks first when the rising side is unbounded rather than bounded. It then compares that gap across two kinds of stake: stakes that confer coercive power over time, and stakes that do not. Each gap is measured within one objective and averaged across the rival-input and knowledge-with-rival-inputs objectives. The gap in the game with non-rival stakes serves as a comparison for any ordinary foraging or raiding that differs between bounded and unbounded rising sides. Subtracting that gap is meant to account for those differences. A single no-reward baseline would cancel out of each gap. Figure 3 lays out H3d’s score as one gap subtracted from another, after a check that the test applies.

Once the rising side’s type can be learned, the commitment account (Fearon 1995; Powell 2006) also predicts less preventive attack against a rising side that is satisfied. By the design’s own labelling rule, H3d is therefore a check on the commitment mechanism. It argues only against a “capability-only” view, in which preventive attack turns on the power shift and the enforcement switch alone. Games with enforceable agreements, random pairings, no-reward rising sides and a rank-seeking rising side serve as checks and controls.

Hypothesis What it claims Main rival Standing
H1 Rank-seeking heirs reach for more Realist security: no difference at equal threat Scored test; on expected counts, can lose but not be supported
H2 Earlier aims predict the kind of killing Strategic and structural accounts: aims add nothing Scored test; the group-targeting arm cannot lose it alone
H3 Knowledge that costs scarce inputs matches resource-seeking on aggression measures within a preset margin “Knowledge is safe” Equivalence check
H3b Training finds the stopping policy — Training check
H3c The stockpiling thresholds are within one level of power conversion “Knowledge is safe” Scored; off-scale thresholds can lose or give an estimate with no verdict, not support
H3d Less preventive attack on a satisfied rising side, where stakes confer power Capability-only view Check on commitment, not a test of aims

Part 3. Leaders are chosen by office, not fame, and aims are read only from records made before the outcome window opens

Who is studied

Fame is measured looking backward. One measure is the space a person gets in reference works (Cattell 1903, used in Cox 1926). Another is the number of Wikipedia language editions with an article on them (Yu et al. 2016; Jara-Figueroa, Yu and Hidalgo 2019). Both are taken after a career is over.

So the main pool is built on holding office instead. It is every effective period in power of a state leader in Archigos 4.1, a dataset of leaders of independent states from 1875 to 2015, compiled without regard to reputation or surviving papers (Goemans, Gleditsch and Chiozza 2009). The study cited here describes the earlier coverage, through 2004. It is linked to leaders’ background information from the LEAD dataset (Ellis, Horowitz and Stam 2015), which I co-authored. Leaders entering after 2004 are hand-coded to LEAD’s rules.

From that pool the design draws a random sample of at least 600 leaders, spread by era, region and type of regime. A translation budget covers each person’s set of documents, called a packet, in languages outside the coding team’s seven reading languages. Results of the coding checks are reported by language group.

Coding follows two routes. Every H1 heir is coded by two independent human coders, and their differences are resolved. Rule 1 scores that resolved human code, reported beside a single coder’s code and the machines’ majority code.

For H2, the machine pipeline codes the part of Archigos with usable documents. The post-1900 roster covers roughly 2,500 periods in power across 2,200 leaders. The 600-leader sample is fully audited by humans. H2 widens from the 600 to the whole pool only if the machines pass their checks (Part 5). If any of the relevant checks fails, H2 stays on the 600.

Samples of the eminent stay in the design as secondary groups. Ends, Rank and Conflict concerns minds of the first rank, and lists of the eminent are where creators who gained administrative or scientific authority are found in bulk.

  • One group is the 301 eminent creators and leaders born between 1450 and 1850 in Cox’s (1926) study.
  • Another is deceased creators born between 1850 and 1950, drawn from the Pantheon dataset. They are checked against Murray’s (2003) Human Accomplishment inventories, which give a second measure of prominence not tied to Wikipedia. The inventories omit government and commerce.

These groups feed a study of people who held delegated authority. They also show how aims differ between the eminent and an unselected roster. Every estimate from them gives worst-case bounds for selection into the list. It also reports how much an unmeasured factor tied to both aims and conduct could affect the estimate (Rosenbaum 2002).

Which papers survived in archives, and which were digitized, filters every sample. So people without usable documents are never dropped silently. The design reports how many people remain at each stage, and bounds that set the missing aims to both extremes. It also reports estimates reweighted for who is missing.

What counts as evidence of aims

Aims are coded only from documents written before a person’s outcome window opens. That window opens at accession, at a first windfall of means, or at the first coded violent act. Each document’s date must be fixable to within a year. Letters, diaries, notebooks, drafts, speeches, manifestos, applications to patrons, prayers and conversations recorded at the time all count. Memoirs and biographies written afterward do not.

A fixed rule chooses each person’s packet: all dated items in the window up to a set number, or a random draw beyond it from a fixed starting number (a “random seed”) so the draw can be repeated. Names of persons, places and offices are replaced by codes. Coders read the packets in a fixed plain-text format. Private writings count for more than public ones or those addressed to patrons.

Every genre has its conventions, and a convention could look like a satiable or rank-seeking aim. So codes for leaders who were not royal are compared against a body of letters by ordinary people of the same era and genre. Hereditary heirs are compared against a separate baseline of royal writings before accession, drawn from across ruling houses and kept separate from the matched group of people who never held top office (described in Part 5).

How aims are coded

Three families of language models code isolated, shuffled passages, with their usual sampling randomness turned off. The majority code stands. The three families share training data, so the design reports how often all three err together, against how often independent errors would.

Coders first sort each stated aim into a final goal or a means to one. If only means appear, the final aim is coded “not stated”. They then code:

  • the aim’s object and whether it is rival;
  • rank-seeking, in a strong or weak degree;
  • boundedness, with “unclear” as its own code;
  • group-targeting, under four limits set out in Ends, Rank and Conflict;
  • needs for resources as means;
  • stated beliefs about threat, competition the leader sees as one side gaining exactly what the other loses and legitimacy, used only as secondary controls.

For H2, a leader’s main aim is the final aim that appears in the most private passages. Ties go to the earliest date, and a model that allows several aims at once serves as a check. Three established methods for reading leaders “at a distance” also run on every passage, as cross-checks (Winter 1993, 2007; Hermann 1980; Walker, Schafer and Young 1998).

What happens to unclear or missing codes?

“Unclear” boundedness is kept as its own level, not dropped. Packets that show only means enter as their own category, neither rank-seeking nor not. Their count is reported, with a planned check that leaves them out. When rank-seeking is genuinely unknown, the design checks the range of estimates obtained by assigning the unknown cases to the two extremes. The main rank-seeking code counts passages about a group’s standing, and mixed passages, as rank-seeking; a narrower code is secondary. It counts only final aims benefiting the individual. Six written rules settle hard cases. For example, a wish for fame with no named person or group as a point of comparison is coded unknown, and coding fame as rank-seeking is reported as a sensitivity check. The pilot tests these rules, and sends them back for repair if they fail, rather than choosing among them. It reports the share classified as rank-seeking both with and without counting fame as rank-seeking.

How conduct is measured

A separate coding run—and, on the human side, a team called team O—codes outside conditions and outcomes without seeing the aims codes. Outside threat is coded from the historical record at accession for all main models. It is also coded period by period during a reign, for the secondary models.

Measuring gains against a leader’s own stated bound would build the bounded-against-unbounded contrast into the outcome. So the design measures holdings instead, in three kinds kept apart:

  • coercive and external holdings: territory and armed force, as the change since accession scaled to the state’s capacity when the leader took office (the main measure);
  • domestic civil growth: budget and staff (reported apart);
  • personal holdings: land, income and extra offices (secondary).

Each holding is compared with what the office normally saw. That “office baseline” is the same change, over a matching stretch of time, for up to two immediate predecessors in the same office. Successors form a second baseline, kept separate because a predecessor’s actions shape what a successor inherits. This baseline uses two successors. First holders of an office, with no predecessor, are left out of the main estimate.

The main outcome I call reaching for more (the technical term is “sought acquisition above baseline”). It is coded present when two things hold. The holder’s gain must exceed the largest gain recorded for the one or two predecessors used in the baseline. And the excess must have been actively sought (asked for, campaigned for, seized or annexed) rather than passively received. It is the only main outcome for Rule 1. A continuous measure of the excess, and a measure of attempts, are reported as secondary. Figure 5 shows the two conditions a holder must meet to be coded as reaching for more.

Turning down an offered increase is a secondary outcome. The design reports it two ways: among those offered, and over all heirs. In the design’s worked comparison, a true odds ratio of 2.2 among those offered shows as about 1.45 over all heirs. At an offer rate of 0.30, 120 to 160 heirs leave only 36 to 48 offered cases.

Standard atrocity datasets define their categories partly by the killers’ goals, which would let aims leak into the outcome. So these datasets are used only to locate events (PITF, Harff 2003; UCDP one-sided violence, Eck and Hultman 2007; Correlates of War territorial change, Tir et al. 1998). Violence is then coded from three facts about behaviour, each tied to a matching quotation from a named source:

  • who was targeted: people who resisted, bore arms or held office, or whole categories of people, including those who complied;
  • whether the killing stopped once the victims submitted;
  • whether the victims’ land or property passed to the killers’ group or state within a set time.

A fixed table combines the first two facts. How targets were selected also splits dispossessive violence into the identity kind and the territory kind. In the first, targets are selected by an identity category. In the second, they are selected for living on or occupying the territory. Whether land or property passed is recorded as a separate fact.

Part 4. The human comparison is an association, causal only under an assumption the record cannot check

Before-and-after comparisons do not work

Comparing the same person before and after gaining power cannot identify the effect of aims. Before an office or a windfall of resources gives someone command authority, a person who lacks that authority has almost no scope for coercive action or acquisition. A before-and-after difference then mostly restates the level after gaining that authority. The code for the aim stated before office is fixed for each person, so a comparison within that person cannot estimate its effect.

Worse, most people who reach high office sought it. Comparing people who campaigned for or seized power mixes up their aims with what got them into office.

The main comparison: heirs who did not choose their moment

The question becomes narrower. Given the same office, did holders with different earlier aims act differently, when the office was not given to them because of their aims? The design has three ways to ask this, ranked by causal strength.

The main one compares heirs across offices, with each heir’s outcome measured against their own office’s predecessors (Figure 6). It compares across offices because most offices supply only one or a few eligible heirs. A natural death in office makes the timing of a succession close to random, but it does not make the successor’s aims random (Jones and Olken 2005). The design therefore keeps only successors fixed by rule before the death, which leaves out contenders who emerged after a vacancy.

Heirs under a fixed hereditary order are reported as their own subgroup. Successors after retirements for ill health, or after contests following a death, enter only the checks and secondary analyses.

Two weaker designs sit beside it:

  • comparing all holders of one office, grouped by how they got in (election, succession, appointment or seizure);
  • comparing people appointed to an office with shortlisted “near misses” who were passed over, according to committee minutes, for reasons unrelated to their aims.

For sitting leaders, discoveries of giant oil and fuel fields give a secondary test of what a sudden windfall does, with stated delays before revenue arrives (Lei and Michaels 2014; Kikuta 2026).

The main estimate uses a statistical model for yes-or-no outcomes (logistic regression) suited to small samples. It compares rank-seeking and other heirs while holding fixed boundedness, route to office, number of predecessors and outside threat at accession. It also uses a summary risk score whose weights are fixed from the pilot before any outcome data are seen, and is reported with and without that score. Its uncertainty calculation also accounts for uncertainty in those weights. As measured, the comparison is an association.

What the formal checks show

Some of the design’s logic was checked by a proof-checking program called Lean. The program confirms only that each conclusion follows from its stated assumptions, not that the assumptions hold in history. In the technical paper, an appendix lists ten of these elementary checks on the design’s logic (Results 1 to 10) and ten sets of figures computed by simulation or by count (Computed 1 to 10). Four of the checks bear on what the heir comparison can show.

  • Result 1. Hold accession threat fixed. The comparison identifies a causal effect of stated aims only if, among heirs who did not choose office, their aims are otherwise unrelated to hidden drivers of acquisition. The historical record cannot verify this assumption.
  • Result 2. The comparison captures the total effect of stated aims, including other people’s responses, only under three conditions. Result 1’s assumption must hold. Neither the accession threat nor the offers made can have answered to the heir’s early writings. And, once the model’s controls are held fixed, offers must be unrelated to any hidden tendency to press for more. For turned-down offers, it holds only among heirs who received offers. Lean models only the threat part.
  • Result 3. Also holding fixed the threat that arose during the reign, as the secondary model does, does not identify an effect of aims. That threat may itself respond to the heir’s aims. Holding it fixed can then create a false contrast even when aims have no direct effect.
  • Result 4. Deterrence by rivals can pull the coded comparison toward 1 when measured against willingness, so a true effect on willingness at or above 2.2 can be coded below 2.2 and scored a loss. Acquisition is the last move in a game where foreign powers and domestic rivals move first: if they read a rank-seeking heir’s early writings or temperament and arm or ally to deter them, the heir may never try to expand and would then be coded as not reaching for more. If other heirs were deterred more instead, the coded comparison could exceed the true willingness effect. Lean shows each case with one example.

Rule 1 scores the total effect, and deterrence is part of that total. Deterrence biases only the measure of willingness. Others’ choices about whom to make offers to can still bias the turned-down-offer comparison.

In a computed illustration of this game, selective offers and appeasement changed the turned-down-offer outcome, especially when counted over all heirs. Offers do not enter the game’s equation for reaching for more. So, by construction, they left reaching for more, and Rule 1’s verdicts, unchanged there.

No statistical model can tell which response governed the historical record. So the design simulates the accession game across all response patterns before seeing the data (Part 8). Beside the main model it reports a plain two-by-two table, labelled as uncorrected for selection, which makes no causal claim and decides nothing.

Two exclusions keep the comparison clean

The main H1 test covers only heads of state or government. People who used authority delegated by a superior sit between the planners and the followers described in Ends, Rank and Conflict. A separate secondary study asks whether such an agent’s aims predict the scale and methods they chose within their remit.

Every person named as an illustration when the conjecture was formed is left out of the test, along with the first list of windfall cases. Frederick II of Prussia publicly renounced conquest and then conquered. He is also left out, and used only as a test item scored by a coder with no stake in the outcome.

The rule that weights private over public passages also requires a final aim to appear in at least one private passage. It is tuned on writings from excluded cases, chosen without regard to their outcomes.

Part 5. Human coders are checked first, then the machines are checked against them

Keeping human coders from recognizing famous subjects

Dates and place names would let a reader who knows history recognize famous subjects and infer their aims from how their careers ended. So the human coders of aims (team E) never code a whole person. Each person’s file is split into dated passages and stripped of names. Passages are shuffled across people and mixed with decoy passages from ordinary writers of the time. On every passage, coders guess the author, to measure how much identity leaks through.

A reliability gate before any machine is judged

Before any machine code is judged, the human coders must pass a reliability gate. Reliability here means agreement between coders, measured by Krippendorff’s alpha (Hayes and Krippendorff 2007). The bar is at least 0.80, with the lower end of its 95 percent range at least 0.67. It applies to the five variables that enter the models: rank-seeking, boundedness and reaching for more for H1, and rank-seeking, resource aim and violence type for H2. Turning down an offer is held to the same target and reported, but is not gated.

This gate is hard to pass even for good coders. One simulation assumed a true reliability of 0.86 and independent errors across variables, with a resource-aim share of 0.20 and equal shares of violence types. On 120 periods, all five variables passed together about 0.22 of the time in one round. They passed 0.66 of the time with one fresh retest per failed variable (Computed 3). Across a range of assumptions the figures were 0.15 to 0.27 and 0.56 to 0.75. Errors shared within a person lowered the main case to 0.12 and 0.50.

The procedure runs in rounds. A development round of about 50 people (120 periods) is used to revise the manual, which is then frozen. The gate round then codes 50 fresh people, plus 120 fresh leaders flagged for violence. The outcomes team checks all 120 for sought gains against their office baselines, and checks 60 for violence type. An equal fresh set is held ready for one retest. Each hypothesis is gated only on its own variables. If a variable fails twice, only the hypotheses that use it stop.

Agreement is not the same as being right. So the pilot also checks known cases. Aims codes must match assessments of those people written before the outcomes. Violence codes on excluded cases such as Jaffa and Saint-Domingue must match an earlier coding, made with the same decision table by a coder with no stake in the outcome.

The machine cannot be blinded, so its errors are tested instead

The machine pipeline uses three model families. Two are fixed versions of leading model families. The third makes its learned settings available, is tuned on hand-coded examples from ordinary writers, and runs on the institution’s own hardware for texts that archives restrict. It is tested against human “gold” files, built by hand from the original documents. Any machine error in finding, transcribing, dating or masking documents therefore counts against the machine.

No check can show that a model reads the passage rather than recalling what it knows of the life. A model that has read the historical literature knows how Napoleon’s reign went. As an analogy only: it is like a juror who has already read the newspapers. Four checks look for signs that knowing the subject’s career affects agreement:

  • passages that run against a figure’s public reputation, where agreement must be within ten points of passages that fit that reputation;
  • splitting results by fame, measured by Wikipedia language editions;
  • asking all three model families to guess each passage’s author;
  • a comparison group of 120 matched people who never held a top office, to see whether agreement rises where there is a known political outcome to remember.

None of these probes establishes blindness. So the gate tests what coding errors would do to the results.

Result 9 shows the key point. Errors whose rates do not depend on the outcome leave a true odds ratio of 1 at 1. Errors that run with the outcome can create a false association, even when overall disagreement looks the same in both outcome groups.

Take an example from the technical paper. Suppose half of each group is truly rank-seeking. In the group that reached for more, wrongly label 10 percent of all cases there as rank-seeking. In the group that did not, wrongly label 10 percent of all cases there as not rank-seeking. That produces an odds ratio of 2.25 from a true 1.00, while showing 10 percent disagreement in both groups. Figure 7 draws this arithmetic example case by case.

So the gate computes the false association the machine’s own errors would create when there is no true effect. It calculates this from how often the machine wrongly adds or misses each relevant aims code in each outcome group. For the acquisition check, it estimates uncertainty by resampling people and offices. The technical term is the “manufactured odds ratio”. The gold set holds 325 periods in office. It samples more cases flagged by signs of acquisition and draws some negative cases from unflagged leaders and heirs. The study reports how prominent the people in the gold set are.

For both rank-seeking and boundedness, the false association must lie between 0.80 and 1.25. Its 90 percent range must lie between 0.67 and 1.50. On the 120 violence-gate leaders, a parallel check asks whether aims-coding errors across violence types create a false association in H2, requiring that score’s 90 percent range to overlap 0.80 to 1.25 (not lie wholly outside it). The make-up of the gold set is my choice, and its pass rates are recomputed before the rules are locked.

The five gated variables are not all tested on the same people. The 325 periods test reaching for more and the false association. Reliability of aims codes is judged on 565 person-periods (one person in one coding window): machine agreement on rank-seeking, boundedness and resource aims must reach at least 0.80 (with a lower bound of 0.67), and on rank-seeking and boundedness it must also come within 0.10 of human-to-human agreement. After at most one revision—written from overall agreement scores and pass-or-fail flags alone—that 0.80 and 0.67 floor is decided on 240 held-back retest periods. Violence type is judged on 120 flagged cases. A fifth of the gold’s predecessor records (280 of 1,400) are also searched by hand, before seeing machine results, to bound holdings the machine might miss.

A sealed human reference team and a live audit

A separate, hand-built benchmark checks the machine’s upstream search and dating of documents. It is needed because in live coding human auditors read the packets the machine retrieved, so any bias in finding or dating documents could still reach the final code.

This human reference arm is 120 people: 60 candidate heirs and 60 leaders after 1900, with 240 predecessor records. It is drawn and sealed in months 1 to 3, before the pipeline exists. An independent team that never sees machine packets or logs then finds, transcribes, masks and codes it entirely by hand. Figure 8 sets the machine’s route for finding records beside the reference team’s route by hand.

It is read once, in month 13, after any pipeline revision is finished. The machine must agree with it at least 90 percent of the time on packet inclusion—whether a person has a usable packet. It must wrongly screen out at most 10 percent of cases the humans included. Its reliability against the reference on rank-seeking and boundedness must be at least 0.80, with a lower bound of 0.67.

Passing every check at once is unlikely even for a good machine. In simulations that assume independent errors and leave out some checks, the gold set had 49 cases that reached for more out of 325. Under those assumptions, a machine as good as a human passes the five simulated variables about 0.22 to 0.24 of the time without revision, and 0.15 to 0.16 with one. With the reference arm’s coding tolerances added (still leaving out its packet-inclusion tolerances), the figures are 0.17 to 0.18 and 0.11 to 0.13 (Computed 4). A machine at the gate’s floor passes about 0.001 of the time or less.

During the main coding, a live audit tracks rolling weekly reliability, monthly pooled false-association scores and a weekly set of 200 test passages. The weekly reliability and monthly false-association scores are compared with the baseline set at entry. In simulation, a floor-level machine with no drift raised a warning in about 0.02 to 0.03 of months. An error pattern creating a false odds ratio near 1.6 was stopped 0.7 to 0.8 of the time once 800 audited periods were pooled, and 0.9 to 0.95 of the time once 1,200 were (Computed 9).

The machine checks decide only one thing: whether H2 widens from the 600-leader sample to the whole pool. H2 stays on the 600 if violence type, rank-seeking or resource aims fails its gate, if rank-seeking fails the reference arm, or if H2’s false-association check fails its bound. H1 rests on double human coding throughout. In the 600-leader sample for H2, every period gets a blind human audit code and human adjudication.

Part 6. The machine study varies what the agents are trained to want

Starting from a known result

The machine study builds on a game by Leibo and colleagues called Gathering (Leibo et al. 2017). Learning agents collect apples, and can fire a beam that tags a rival and removes it for a while. Tagging earns no reward, so competing for apples is the only reason to tag. Agents that learned where apples were scarce became more aggressive than those that learned where apples were plentiful. Leibo and colleagues held the agents’ reward fixed, and this design varies it. Before the rules are locked, the pilot fixes how the learners are built, how many play in each episode, what types play, and how their fellow players are chosen.

Five factors crossed

The core experiment crosses five factors (Figure 9a):

  1. Objective. There are four. Non-rival knowledge rewards discovering fixed hidden sites, and one agent’s discovery takes nothing from another’s. The reward is paid once per site and excludes agents’ positions. Rank rewards an agent’s score minus the average of the others’. Rival input rewards consuming a resource that runs out. Knowledge with rival inputs rewards discovering a site, but each discovery spends a scarce instrument. That is the worrying case from Changing the Ends.
  2. Boundedness. Each objective runs with no cap and with a finite cap. The agent can see its progress toward the cap.
  3. Scarcity. The scarce resource regrows at three different rates.
  4. Power conversion. Progress earns units of a separate weapons stock that makes tagging cheaper or extends its range. The design matches earning rates for competent agents playing alone across objectives, and the stock never changes how fast apples regrow. It captures, in miniature, an argument from Powell (1991).
  5. Raiding. Each agent keeps what it collects, and its weapons stock, in a home store that is drawn down at a fixed rate. Rival-input reward is paid when the resource is consumed, so stores buffer against future scarcity and a raided unit is lost reward. Having no setting that pays on collection instead is a stated limit. With raiding off, stores are safe. With raiding on, an agent standing on an unguarded rival store takes from it. That creates a security dilemma in which stores are both buffers and prey (Hirshleifer 1995; Jervis 1978).

Two details guard the knowledge and rank objectives. A curiosity reward based on surprise runs only as a separate, labelled arm (after Schmidhuber 2010). Under such a reward other agents are the main source of surprise, so tagging would be an artefact of the reward. For rank, a bonus for coming first is used only as a fallback, if the main rank reward fails a solo skill test. Results in the rank games speak only to the specification fixed.

Keeping skill from masquerading as aims

Differences in learned skill, or in the size of rewards, could look like effects of aims. To prevent this:

  • rewards are scaled to match across objectives in solo play;
  • agents train until they pass a solo skill threshold, not for a fixed time;
  • frozen agents must pass solo tests of foraging, navigation and tagging accuracy before entering the shared games.

An exploratory probe of the kind Imas, Koh and Legg (2026) propose also measures how each frozen agent performs across identical copies. One comparison holds computing power per copy fixed, and another holds total computing power fixed.

Every outcome is behaviour: tags per step, exclusions, damage, raids, time spent guarding, stockpiling before the bound and acquisition after it, and bargaining moves. None is a stated persona. Language-model agents in negotiation games such as Welfare Diplomacy (Mukobi et al. 2023), GovSim (Piatti et al. 2024) and Diplomacy (Bakhtin et al. 2022) are exploratory only. An objective given to such a model as an instruction is a persona by another route. Figure 10 draws the home store’s route with raiding off and with raiding on.

The main comparison and its controls

H3’s main comparison asks whether, in the shared games with raiding off, the knowledge-with-rival-inputs objective is as aggressive across scarcity, and as responsive to power conversion, as the rival-input objective. This is what the reading of convergence in Changing the Ends predicts. H3 loses when the whole 95 percent interval for any of the three gaps lies outside the margin, in either direction. The margin is one quarter of the rival-input objective’s scarcity effect measured in the pilot, converted by a fixed rule.

The pure-knowledge game is a negative control. There, tagging and weapons buy nothing except protection of discovery time from rivals’ tags. A separate version removes even that interruption. The rank game is a positive control, because tagging lowers rivals’ scores and so raises rank reward by construction. Neither decides H3.

The further arms

H3b checks whether a bounded objective trains in at all, with no power conversion and no raiding. Doing nothing is free, each other action has a small cost, and nothing is paid after the bound. By Result 10, stopping at the bound is then strictly better than taking any finite positive number of further costly actions.

At the bound, a stand-in trained with no reward under the same cost takes over in that exact state. The bound may leave the agent in places such a stand-in rarely saw in training. So a stand-in trained from random mid-game starting points is reported beside it. If any objective has a 95 percent interval for extra acquisition over the stand-in that lies wholly above the margin, H3b loses and the objective is named. The margin is set from run-to-run variation across random seeds (separate training runs from different random starting numbers) in the pilot.

H3b asks only whether training finds the policy Result 10 makes best in these environments. It does not settle the broader limit stated in Limits, and an Answer. Nor does it test goals going wrong when the setting changes after training (Langosco et al. 2022). An early-fixed rank cap can also conflict with keeping one’s standing, a stated limit.

H3c runs the four bounded objectives at five levels of power conversion: none, a quarter, a half, three quarters and full. It runs them at middle scarcity, with raiding off and with raiding on. It fits a curve that can only rise, to find where stockpiling before the bound first passes the margin. With raiding off, the comparison is a negative check.

H3d uses a two-agent bargaining game. It has explicit offer, accept and transfer moves, a scheduled and announced rise in one side’s power, and a stake that either confers weapons power over time or gives only non-rival reward. A switch makes agreements either enforced or unenforceable.

Beside learning agents that do not plan, the design runs planning agents. These choose moves by searching ahead in the game’s simulator, using a learned value estimate and a learned model of the opponent; they are never given the opponent’s true policy. This adapts the work of Schrittwieser et al. (2020), whose planner searched a learned model rather than the simulator. They run at short and long horizons.

How big is the machine study?

Each game setting runs with at least ten random seeds, set from pilot variation. There are 268 settings in all: 190 for learning agents that do not plan and 78 for planning agents. Of these, 84 are confirmatory, and an independent laboratory re-runs all 84. By Computed 10, the 268 settings need about 64,600 hours of graphics-processor time at ten seeds each, with a reserve of 27,000 hours. Sizing for H3c gives 11, 25 and 34 seeds per scored dose setting when run-to-run spread (the standard deviation) is 0.20, 0.30 and 0.35.

Part 7. Each hypothesis is scored by rules fixed before any confirmatory data are read

Locking the rules in two stages

To keep choices from bending toward the findings (Nosek et al. 2018; Monogan 2013), everything is deposited in advance on the Open Science Framework, in two stages. That covers the design, codebooks, sampling lists, quantities to estimate and decision rules.

An independent referee reviews each stage before deposit. The referee has no stake in this series or in LEAD, and is told that I co-authored LEAD and formulated the conjecture under test.

  • The rules for admitting human-side coding, the reference arm’s tolerances and the matching rule for the comparison group are locked at the end of month 9, before any test gold is read.
  • The machine study is deposited in month 10, after the pilot fixes its settings and before the first confirmatory run in month 11. The pilot also fixes the solo skill requirements and the number of training runs per setting before deposit.
  • The human study is deposited in months 13 to 14, after the human gate, the machine gate and the single reading of the reference arm. It carries the simulation of others’ responses, run before the data. Figure 11 lays these planned steps out month by month; none has yet been done.

In the technical paper, a table sorts every number that bears on a verdict into three kinds: fixed now, fixed by rule at the lock, or recomputed before deposit. For secondary comparisons, a procedure sets a target of 5 percent for the expected share of false positives among results flagged as significant (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995).

Three verdicts, one hypothesis at a time

Each hypothesis is scored on its own, and the conjecture as a whole gets no single verdict. A hypothesis can be scored as lost or supported. Under estimation, the study reports what it can estimate and gives no verdict. The rules lean on intervals, meaning the range of values compatible with the data at a stated level of confidence.

Rule 1 (H1). H1 is scored on the resolved double-human code, on reaching for more alone, in the direction where the conjecture predicts an odds ratio above 1 (Figure 12). H1 is lost if the 95 percent interval lies wholly below 2.2, or wholly on the wrong side of 1. The loss rule comes first.

The bar of 2.2 is my choice of the smallest effect worth detecting, fixed in advance and read on the observed scale. I know of no earlier result that fixes such a bar for acquisition. Where 49 in 325 of the heirs without rank-seeking aims reach for more, an odds ratio of 2.2 means the rank-seeking group is about 1.9 times as likely to (Result 8). The expected weakening from coding error is stated in advance, and a corrected estimate is reported beside the observed one. The study also states the error rates implied by that expected weakening before the test. Verdicts at bars of 1.5 and 1.8 are reported too.

H1 is supported only if it is not lost and the interval excludes 1 in the conjecture’s direction. Support comes in two forms: a nonzero effect not shown to be smaller than 2.2, or, only when the whole interval sits at or above 2.2, an effect at or above 2.2. Results 6 and 7 checked the earlier rule, which used two outcomes.

The stronger form is hard to reach. At 210 heirs per group and a 15 percent base rate, its chance was 0.023 at a true odds ratio of 2.2, 0.247 at 3.0 and 0.731 at 4.0 (Computed 7). If neither the loss nor the support rule applies, the result is estimation. On the expected sample, H1 falls into the fallback described in Part 8, where it can lose but cannot be supported.

A loss never shows that aims do not matter (Result 5). An interval from 1.5 to 2.0, say, lies wholly below 2.2 and still excludes no effect. Such a result is labelled a loss against the conjecture’s bar, but evidence against the realist rival’s prediction of no effect.

Rule 2 (H2). Add the leader’s main earlier aim to a model that already has the strategic situation and the five non-ideological Harff factors. Then ask how much better that model predicts the type of violence in data it was not fitted on. The data are split by country, with uncertainty also estimated by country. The two models are scored on the same held-out cases, using the probabilities they assigned to the kinds of violence that actually occurred. The study averages the difference per case and corrects the uncertainty calculation for the paired comparison. H2 is lost if the 95 percent interval for that gain lies wholly below a smallest meaningful gain, fixed from the pilot before the lock.

H2 is also lost if either of the two main links (rank-seeking to coercive, or resource aims to violence over territory) has a 95 percent interval wholly on the wrong side of 1. For each link, 1 means equal predicted probabilities after adjusting for the other factors. The rare group-targeting link cannot lose H2 alone. When neither loss condition holds and the 95 percent interval for the gain lies wholly above zero, H2 is supported on the machine-coded pool only if the rank-seeking-to-coercive point estimate lies above 1 in both the whole pool and the human-audited 600; otherwise the result is estimation, with both estimates reported.

Rule 3 (H3). H3 is lost if, on any of three measures, the gap between the two objectives lies wholly outside the margin. The three are average aggression, how aggression rises with scarcity, and how much power conversion raises it. The change with scarcity is measured as the slope of a straight-line trend. Rule 3 is scored in the unbounded games with raiding off for the non-planning learning agents, using 95 percent intervals for loss. H3 is supported only if all three gaps lie wholly inside the margin, at 90 percent intervals. Because all three checks must pass, the rule applies no extra adjustment for multiple comparisons. Otherwise the result is estimation.

Rule 4 (H3b). With no power conversion and no raiding, H3b is lost if, for any of the four objectives, the 95 percent interval for bounded agents’ acquisition after the bound minus the stand-in’s (averaged across the three scarcity levels) lies wholly above the margin. The failing objective is named. Support needs the 90 percent interval wholly below the margin for every objective; otherwise the result is estimation.

Rule 5 (H3c). H3c is lost if, with raiding off or on, the 95 percent interval for the gap between the two objectives’ thresholds lies wholly outside one dose level. So if a knowledge agent never stockpiles beyond the margin, while the 95 percent upper bound on the resource agent’s threshold lies below three quarters, H3c loses. For scoring, an agent that never crosses the margin is recorded at full conversion, and one already beyond it at zero is recorded at zero. Support needs raiding on, both thresholds strictly inside the scale, and the 90 percent interval for their gap wholly within one dose level. With raiding off, the pure-knowledge threshold is expected to run off the top of the scale. A threshold inside the scale there is reported as an anomaly against how the environment was built.

Rule 6 (H3d). First the rule asks whether the test applies. The trained unbounded rising side may exploit the shift in fewer than 0.30 of test games against a scripted opponent that does not attack. Or the check that enforcement works may fail. In either case H3d is estimation and no verdict is given. Otherwise, H3d is lost if the 95 percent interval for that difference of differences lies wholly below 0.15 or wholly below zero. It is supported only if no loss condition holds and the 95 percent interval excludes zero in the predicted direction.

Part 8. On expected counts, the main human test can lose but cannot be supported

The archive probably holds too few heirs

Three things bound what the human study can conclude: how many qualifying heirs the archive holds, coding error, and how others responded to those heirs in life.

The design aims for 420 heirs, 210 per group. In the simplest version of the model, at a 15 percent base rate of reaching for more, the rule then supported a true 2.2 with probability 0.905 and wrongly lost it with probability 0.026 (Computed 1). This simulation used rank-seeking alone to predict reaching for more. At a 10 percent base rate, support was 0.798. The 420 target is kept as a margin of safety.

The historical record is not expected to supply 420. A desk count on Archigos 4.1 found 3,409 periods in power, with 202 exits by natural death and 68 by retirement for ill health, and 269 successors in all (Computed 2). The ill-health cases are set aside for checks. The projection allows for roughly 130 hereditary accessions. That is a provisional allowance pending the feasibility count of heirs in each political entity. That 130 is worked back from a budget for screening about 400 candidates, counted before overlaps are removed. Separately, the 15 percent base rate used in sizing sits beside a rate of about one in three at which a holder would beat the larger of two interchangeable predecessors’ gains by chance alone, before asking whether the gain was sought. The design reports the chance that the test would detect the assumed effect at several baseline rates of reaching for more. A working guess is made that 60 to 80 percent of successors were fixed by rule, and that documents can be found for 60 percent. That leaves about 120 to 160 heirs.

At that size, at a 0.35 rank-seeking share and a 15 percent base rate, support at a true 2.2 in that simplest model would be only 0.40 to 0.51 if allowed (0.39 to 0.48 at a 0.30 share, and 0.35 to 0.44 at 140 heirs in an adjusted illustration). At a 15 percent base rate, example 95 percent intervals around a true 2.2 stretch from as low as 0.82 to as high as 5.38.

A fallback fixed in advance

So a fallback is locked in before any confirmatory code is read. The fallback is triggered by either of two findings. The pilot’s screen may count fewer than 420 eligible heirs with usable documents. Or a simulation at the pilot’s measured rates may put the power to support below 0.70. That simulation runs before deposit and uses both the measured outcome rates and the measured share of rank-seeking heirs. In either case H1 becomes estimation with a bound on the effect’s size.

Under the fallback only support is withheld, and the loss rule applies unchanged. At 75 heirs per group and no true effect, the test registered a loss 0.412 of the time at a 15 percent base rate and 0.311 at 10 percent. Estimation was the usual verdict.

For H2, the question is how much machine coding of the whole pool adds. Projections rest on inputs that stay assumptions until the pilot measures them. On those projections, machine-coding the whole pool after 1900 yields about 370 cases of violence beyond the office norm, against about 90 in the 600-leader sample (Computed 8). After allowing for clustering within countries and for coding error at the gate’s floor, that becomes about 200 to 260 effective cases against about 80, a gain of two and a half to three times. The group-targeting arm stays too small on either route, at about 4 to 9 cases in the sample and 18 to 37 in the pool.

Coding error weakens the estimate, and others’ responses can move it

Errors in coding aims weaken the observed odds ratio, which raises the chance of a false loss against the 2.2 bar. At a 0.35 rank-seeking share and a 15 percent base rate, a true 2.2 is observed as about 2.09 with human coders at reliability 0.86 (Computed 5). It is observed as 1.93 to 1.98 at the machine floor, and 1.74 at reliability 0.67. Figure 13 plots these three observed values against the true 2.2.

At 420 heirs, simulated miscoding reduced support from 0.882 to 0.841 at the human level, to between 0.751 and 0.787 at the machine floor, and to 0.612 at reliability 0.67. It raised wrong loss from 0.025 to 0.039, to between 0.059 and 0.076, and to 0.155 at the same three levels. H1 uses double human coding, so its code is weakened at the human rate.

Others’ strategic responses can also move the result. The design tried them in an illustrative game: 210 per group, three in ten heirs offered an increase, half of the offered rank-seeking heirs refusing it, and no coding error (Computed 6). Without deterrence, a true willingness effect of 2.2 was lost about 0.02 to 0.03 of the time.

In this example, deterring heirs judged most likely to press for more lowered the total effect. The losses counted here are relative to willingness. When others deterred half of the heirs they judged most likely to press for more, the total odds ratio fell to about 1.65 when judged by temperament and to about 1.11 when judged also from the heir’s writings. Losses against willingness rose to 0.17 and 0.68. Because deterrence is part of the total effect Rule 1 scores, and that total lies below 2.2 in both cases, these are losses against willingness, not against the scored total.

With no true effect on willingness, false support reached 0.028 when deterrence went by temperament. Selective offers and appeasement changed only the secondary turned-down-offer outcome, because offers do not enter reaching for more in the game. The full simulation, run before the main coding, covers 1,536 grid settings plus 512 calibrated to the pilot’s and gate’s measured rates.

Fund the feasibility stage first

Whether H2 can widen beyond the 600 is a live risk. In simulation, admission for H2 was 0.40 to 0.68 for a machine as good as a human without revision, and 0.34 to 0.64 with one (Computed 4). These simulations used 49 positive cases in 325. That range spans the two readings of the gate’s rules that remain unsettled. For a machine at the gate’s floor it was 0.01 to 0.03. These figures depend on checks outside the simulation, and are recomputed before the lock.

So a feasibility stage, Phase 0, comes first, before the main human-study money is released. It completes the following:

  • the count of eligible heirs and of the pool;
  • a pilot of how many documents can be found;
  • the human reliability gate;
  • the machine gate and the hand search of predecessor records;
  • the comparison with the reference arm;
  • the machine study’s calibration and its check that the settings work as intended;
  • both pre-registration deposits.

Part 9. What the design cannot show

It studies planners, not followers

The historical record here is a record of planners. The second layer of atrocity is missing from Archigos, Cox and Pantheon: the followers whose refusal, as argued in Ends, Rank and Conflict, was the historical check. This design says nothing about them. The secondary study of agents reaches a middle position, delegated authority. I left that position outside the argument there and label the secondary study accordingly. Figure 14 sets the three levels of authority beside what the design studies at each.

Aims are inferred from what people wrote

The design weights private over public writing and norms codes against writing of the same era and genre. It tunes the weighting on excluded cases and runs other measures of motive alongside. Even so, a person who never wrote down their final aims is coded “not stated”. A person who hid their aims in private papers as well as public ones is misclassified.

Reliability measures agreement between coders, not truth. The check against known cases is the only check of validity. On the aims side it rests on assessments written before the outcomes, which are sparser than later accounts. On the violence side it rests on one earlier coding by a coder with no stake. Several historical and bibliographic background claims in the design were checked only against the record.

A language model cannot be blinded

For H2’s whole pool, the codes come from machines that have read the biographies. The checks can show whether the machine codes agree with human codes made from the original documents, whether outcome-linked errors stay within the bounds the gold can resolve, and whether the machines’ packet-inclusion decisions agree with the independent human team’s.

None of the checks can show that the agreement comes from the passage, rather than from biographical knowledge that the models and the human gold coders share. Contamination that runs evenly across outcome groups, and that the gold shares, passes every test here. The probes and the 120-person comparison group show whether agreement rises where there is a political outcome to know. They cannot prove that what remains is read from the text alone.

Double human coding for H1, H2’s fallback to the 600, and three side-by-side H1 estimates are remedies for what the checks can see. They are not remedies for what the checks cannot see.

Much of the design is procedure that has not yet run

Every yield of documents, base rate, pool count, error rate, hour figure and staff availability used here is an assumption until the pilot measures it. That includes H2’s gain in effective cases. An option in a contract to hire coders is not capacity. A contingency line in the budget is not committed money or named people.

The simulations of the gates assume errors independent across variables, with one sensitivity run that shares the machine’s errors across aims codes. They also leave out some checks. Those unmodelled checks are prior human coder reliability, agreement on passages that run against reputation, and the reference arm’s packet-inclusion tolerances. The live-audit simulations treat person-periods as independent rather than grouped within persons. They assume that 25 percent of cases fall in the positive outcome group, and leave individual subgroups (strata) with fewer than 1,200 audited periods without a pooled test for differences across subgroups.

Releasing only overall scores and pass-or-fail flags after the first gate run still gives feedback. A revision aimed at overall agreement can shift outcome-linked error while overall agreement stays flat. The check on the 120 held-back outcome units catches only a large shift, and cannot settle the full false-association bound.

Several tools handle missing archives. Stage-by-stage counts, a pre-registered test of whether document yield predicts the outcome, and reweighting are all sensitivity checks; the yield test is reported and changes no verdict. Nothing here shows that what failed to survive in archives, or remains undigitized, can be ignored. The design answers its critics by scheduling and pricing a validation, not by reporting one done.

The comparison is not an experiment

On the human side, identification rests on comparisons across offices under nearly random timing of accession, plus secondary comparisons within offices. It does not rest on random assignment of aims. Heirs are a small and unusual population, whose spread by era and region is reported once the pilot lists them.

Successors after a natural death are close to random in timing, not in who they are. That is why only those fixed by rule before the death enter the main test. Near misses exist only where committees kept minutes. Every estimate about leaders is conditional on holding office. Each carries sensitivity bounds for hidden confounding (Rosenbaum 2002) and worst-case bounds for missing documents. The sensitivity bounds compare leaders matched for this check. If an heir reached their stated stopping point and still sought and gained holdings above the office baseline for security reasons the outside-threat measure missed, Rule 1 still counts that outcome against the hypothesis. This is the distinction between a satisfied aim and continued demand I draw in Satiation Is Not Enough.

The record is uneven

The record is uneven across eras, languages and sexes. Cox’s study ends with people born in 1850, while Archigos begins in 1875. Violence coding is primary from 1955, with 1900–1954 secondary, and Harff’s (2003) structural factors were first fitted on state failures between 1955 and 1997. Pantheon reflects what Wikipedia’s editors chose to write about.

Women are a small fraction of every population (on European states led by queens, see Dube and Harish 2020), and differences by sex cannot be estimated here. And no human aim in the record names humanity as a whole. The group-targeting arm of H2 is tested only on aims that name a group. It never reaches the case that, as Ends, Rank and Conflict notes, has no historical counterpart: a group-targeting aim that names everyone.

The machine games are small sandboxes

The site-discovery, weapons and bargaining games are simplified stand-ins for conflict. Only the reinforcement-learning agents carry their objectives in their trained weights. A clean result would show that what an objective asks for can matter for learned behaviour, at fixed solo skill. It would not show that any frontier system’s aims are of a particular type, or that satiable aims survive when a system modifies itself.
